Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Investment and Governance: Through The Lens of Sustainability
Jitendra Aswani and Roberto Rigobon
NBER Working Paper No. 36011
November 2026
JEL No. G30
ABSTRACT
Using 3,944 sustainable bond issuances by public firms from 2013 to 2022, we examine the causal 
effect of sustainable investment on governance adoption. A heteroskedasticity-based identification 
strategy reveals that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (by total debt) raises the likelihood of 
sustainable governance adoption by 9.2%. Such adoption improves environmental performance by 
16% (structural estimates). These effects are confined to non-financial firms; for financial firms, 
governance adoption alone is in-sufficient, as sustainable loan borrowers environmental 
performance does not improve. Firms with stronger environmental performance are less likely to 
adopt sustainable governance. Results are robust to alternative definitions and extensive 
specification checks.

1. INTRODUCTION
Achieving global climate objectives necessitates targeted financial commitments. According
to one estimate, a monumental investment exceeding $270 trillion is required for decar-
bonization efforts to realize the net-zero ambitions by 2050, which translates to an annual
investment of around $9.4 trillion.1 The global fixed income market stands as a pivotal pil-
lar for gathering the requisite capital for this climate transition. In 2022 alone, this market
reached an unprecedented total of $122 trillion, with the corporate debt sector contribut-
ing about 32%. Within this context, sustainable debt has experienced a significant surge,
reaching $3.7 trillion, with corporate sustainable debt comprising approximately half of this
amount, or about $1.7 trillion.2
Given the pivotal role of corporate sustainable debt in facilitating the transition to a
more climate-resilient economy, existing research predominantly focuses on clarifying the
phenomenon of greenium (Flammer [2021]; P´astor et al. [2022]; Aswani and Rajgopal [2025])
or on delving into the investment preferences of stakeholders within this sector (refer to Baker
et al. [2022], Hartzmark and Sussman [2019]). Nevertheless, the efficacy of governance prac-
tices plays a critical role in determining whether investments are channelled solely towards
financial gains or whether they also address and reduce a firm’s adverse environmental im-
pacts. In this paper, we explore this under-researched area by investigating whether sus-
tainable investment motivates firms to make changes in their organizational structure, such
as adopting sustainable governance. Drawing on the extensive literature on signaling in
economics, finance, and related disciplines3, we hypothesize that firms that care about sus-
tainable investment would undertake necessary changes in their organizational structure to
signal their commitment to the market, even if such signals are costly. Firms would adopt
these governance changes because sustainable debt issuance requires reporting compliance,
which includes the development of impact reports, use-of-proceeds accounts, and third-party
certifications required under green bond principles. These changes in governance would help
achieve compliance levels and attain the targeted environmental performance. Therefore,
these governance changes would be an observable signal for investors that firms are serious
about implementing sustainable projects.
As the literature on the governance impact of investment shows, firms alter corporate

catastrophe-risk/decarbonisation-tracker.html
2Based on projections from a Bloomberg report, Global ESG Assets are expected to reach $40 trillion by
2030, largely driven by ESG funds and sustainable debt mechanisms.
3See Kreps and Sobel [1994] for a literature review.
1
governance to attract more investment and to reduce the cost of debt. Due to a simultaneity
issue, it is difficult to determine whether the firm is signaling to existing investors or at-
tempting to attract new investments. We address this simultaneity issue using identification
through heteroskedasticity and demonstrate that sustainable investment leads to changes
in sustainable governance. Furthermore, we provide causal evidence on whether a firm’s
adoption of sustainable governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and, more
importantly, mitigates negative externalities, or if it merely serves as an advertising gimmick
that supports greenwashing claims.
Corporations engage in sustainable debt financing through two principal methods: they
either commit to dedicating the funds solely to environmentally friendly projects or opt to
tie the cost of borrowing to future environmental risks. The market segment characterized
by restrictions on the use of proceeds typically features participation from large, financially
robust firms with superior credit ratings (Aswani and Rajgopal [2025]). Green bonds, social
bonds, and sustainability bonds fall under this category. In contrast, sustainable debt in-
struments (such as sustainability-linked bonds) that integrate environmental risk into bond
features see more diverse participation across various industry sectors. Issuers of these bonds
adhere to restrictions on the use of funds, which are limited to specific categories, includ-
ing Energy, Energy Efficiency, Green Buildings and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Forestry,
Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation, Waste Management, Clean Water, Pollution
Control, and Circular Economy, as outlined in the Green Bond Principles. To monitor the
development of these green projects, firms need to implement changes in governance for the
management of proceeds and to evaluate the impact of these projects.
To empirically examine whether sustainable investment motivates firms to adopt sus-
tainable governance, we gather sustainable fixed income data from the Bloomberg Global
Fixed Income and Environmental Finance databases, with sustainability governance metrics
extracted from BoardEx. Additionally, we collect data on firm fundamentals from World-
scope and Global Compustat. Upon merging these databases, the final dataset comprises
6,925 firms from 2013 to 2022, yielding 59,019 firm-year observations. Of these, 30% (3,053
firms) have implemented significant organizational changes to promote sustainability during
the observed period. Our sample also includes sustainable debt issuers that issued 3,944 sus-
tainable bonds between 2013 and 2022. Of these issuances, 3,056 are green bonds, with the
remainder comprising other sustainable debt instruments. The sample firms are primarily
from the financial, industrial, healthcare, materials, and consumer discretionary sectors. Ge-
ographically, a significant portion of these sustainable firms are located in the United States,
2
the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Canada, and Australia. This geographical distribu-
tion closely mirrors the distribution of issuers of sustainable debt, which is predominantly
from the United States, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and China, suggesting a
correlation between organizational sustainability changes and sustainable debt issuance.
To evaluate sustainable debt at the firm-year level, we consider two indicators: the ratio
of cumulative sustainable debt issued (scaled by total debt) and the natural logarithm of the
total number of sustainable bonds issued. We define sustainable governance using a binary
variable that equals 1 for firms that appoint a chief sustainability officer (CSO) or establish
a sustainability committee, and 0 otherwise. To enhance the validity of our governance
metrics, we supplement our analysis with data from the Refinitiv ESG database. To test
our hypothesis, we conduct panel regressions with country, year, and industry fixed effects.
We find that a 1% increase in the amount of sustainable debt (as a proportion of total debt
issued) improves sustainable governance by 9.2%. These results suggest that sustainable
debt issuances inspire firms to introduce organizational changes for sustainability, paving
the way for sustainable governance. We are aware of endogeneity concerns, particularly
reverse causality. A firm that undertakes organizational change to achieve sustainability
may increase the issuance of sustainable debt, rather than issuing sustainable debt which
triggers the firm to introduce organizational change. We confirm the endogeneity problem
by regressing sustainable debt on organizational change; we find that the latter increases the
amount of sustainable debt (scaled) by 4.1%.
To mitigate endogeneity concerns, we use identification through heteroskedasticity (see
Rigobon [2003] and Rigobon and Sack [2003]) and generate causal generalized method of
moments (GMM) estimates. The literature on identification through heteroskedasticity sug-
gests that a system of simultaneous equations can be resolved due to a change in variance
of one variable with respect to another, even if there are more unknowns than knowns. The
simplest intuition can be gained by considering a special case: splitting the sample into two
regimes and assuming that in the second regime, sustainable governance is more volatile than
in the first, while the variance in sustainable debt issuances remains constant across the two
regimes. This increase in the variance of sustainable governance implies that the cloud of
realizations enlarges through the sustainable debt schedule. The residuals are distributed
over an ellipse, and the shift in the variance implies a tilting toward the sustainable debt
curve. From the instrumental variables perspective, this is equivalent to having a proba-
bilistic instrument. In sum, if both variances shift by the same amount, the system is not
identified. On the other hand, the system can be identified by the difference in relative
3
variance between the two regimes for sustainable debt issuances and sustainable governance.
For a robust exogenous analysis of regime shifts and parameter stability, we leverage
the unforeseen emergence of the novel coronavirus and the ensuing economic downturn that
began in February 2020. We divide our dataset into three periods surrounding this event:
2013-2018, 2019-2020, and 2021-2022. From a methodological standpoint, this division acts
as a form of probabilistic instrument; in the first regime, we cannot definitively assert that
there is a shift in the pattern of organizational changes. However, in the second regime, the
dynamics of organizational change are noticeably altered as a result of the shock, allowing us
to more accurately discern the relationship between organizational changes and sustainable
debt issuances. The third regime helps us to test the stability of the structural parameters,
and we show that our results are robust to any combination of regimes and close to an
all-regime model.
Upon generating the causal generalized method of moments (GMM)estimates, we find
that a 1% increase in the amount of sustainable debt issuance increases the probability of
adoption of sustainable governance by 9.2%. These findings are statistically significant at
the 1% level. We confirm these results using the number of sustainable bond issuances as
an alternative proxy for the sustainable debt measure. These results show that OLS under-
estimates the causal effect because simultaneity biases the coefficient toward zero. The true
causal effect is 67% larger than the naive estimate. This implies that studies and policy eval-
uations that used ordinary least square (OLS) to assess the governance impact of green bond
markets under-estimate the real organizational impact by approximately two-thirds. Addi-
tionally, we observe that superior governance tends to attract increased investment, a finding
well-documented in the prior literature. This indicates that, particularly when addressing
the endogenous nature of investment and governance, investment also drives governance
improvements, not just the other way around. Our methodology causally demonstrates this.
Our results also show that investment drives governance more strongly than governance
drives investment (9.2% versus 4.2%) which suggests that the traditional view in corporate
finance, that governance reforms are needed to attract investment, is incomplete for sustain-
able markets. These results provide evidence that organizational reform follows capital flows
This reversal of the conventional governance-investment sequence has implications for how
regulators should sequence policy interventions: mandating sustainable debt instruments
may be more effective at inducing governance reform than mandating governance structures
to attract sustainable capital.
Although our GMM estimates are comparable to Iliev and Roth [2023] which find that
4
director exposure to foreign ESG regulation increases the probability of ESG committee
formation by approximately 8–12 percentage points. Our methodology for identification
dominates the quasi-natural experiment used in Iliev and Roth [2023] because latter suf-
fers from verification issue of exclusion restriction, instrument intensity, and the deviation
of Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) from Average Treatment Effect (ATE). The
identification through heteroskedasticity is free from such issues.4
Beyond addressing endogeneity concerns, we expand our analysis through a series of
additional tests. Aswani and Rajgopal [2025] suggests that the market shows a preference
for sustainable bonds issued by firms in the financial sector, as evidenced by a positive
shareholder reaction and the presence of a greenium in the secondary market. Therefore,
we specifically examine the impact within financial and high-pollution sectors. Our findings
indicate a more pronounced effect among financial sector firms compared to those in polluting
sectors.
Considering that shareholder rights differ across jurisdictions (see Porta et al. [1998]),
we further dissect our results based on the legal framework of the firms’ home countries,
distinguishing between common law and civil law systems. Our analysis demonstrates that
our findings hold particularly strongly in civil law countries, which typically feature weaker
corporate governance systems compared to their common law counterparts. We show that, in
such countries, investment inspires governance more strongly than in common law countries,
where investors are protected by law.
In the second part of the paper, we evaluate whether a firm’s adoption of sustainable
governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and, more importantly, mitigates
negative externalities. We contend that sustainable governance serves as a complementary
monitoring tool alongside shareholder oversight of a firm’s sustainability efforts. Further-
more, we assert that for firms engaged in sustainable investing, implementing sustainable
governance is unlikely to be merely a marketing strategy, due to the associated costs and the
existing monitoring conducted by pro-social shareholders. With this perspective in mind,
we assess the impact of sustainable governance on the firm’s future sustainable performance.
Our results indicate that sustainable governance can enhance a firm’s environmental per-
formance by 16% to 18%. These results are 2.5–4 times larger than Dyck et al. [2023]’s
estimates which find that adoption of majority voting for directors increases future environ-
mental performance scores by approximately 4–7 percentage points (depending on specifica-
tion). However, in our results, this improvement in environmental performance is limited to
4For further details, refer section 5.1.1.
5
non-financial firms. When we analyzed the environmental performance of sustainable loan
borrowers who borrowed the amount from financial firms that issued sustainable debt and
made changes in sustainable governance, we did not find significant improvement. In con-
trast, we find that GMM estimates for environmental performance in relation to sustainable
governance are insignificant, implying that firms with better environmental performance have
a lower chance of adopting sustainable governance. These results are intuitive, as firms with
better environmental performance would not adopt sustainable governance if the benefits
are marginal compared to the cost of adoption.
Our research draws parallels with Starmans et al. [2026] and Wintoki et al. [2012]. A
recent theory paper by Starmans et al. [2026] predicts that sustainable investing can weaken
the governance role of financial markets by reducing the sensitivity of stock prices to infor-
mation about firm fundamentals, particularly when firm externalities are significant. The
authors hypothesize that pro-social investors would exit firms with weak environmental and
social (E & S) performance even if the firms have exceptional financial performance. It
would lead to a decline in informed trading, reduce price informativeness, and lower a firm’s
financial performance. In our work, we show that sustainable investment motivates firms to
adopt sustainable governance practices, thereby improving their sustainable performance.
Wintoki et al. [2012] revisits the relationship between board structure and firm perfor-
mance using the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator, concluding that there is
no causal link between board structure and contemporaneous firm performance. This study
importantly highlights the biases inherent in traditional estimators that neglect the dynamic
interplay between current governance structures and historical firm performance. In a vein
similar to Wintoki et al. [2012], our application of the GMM model, particularly identified
by heteroskedasticity, demonstrates that changes in the sustainable governance structure
improve sustainable performance. We also show that investment significantly encourages
firms to augment governance practices, rather than the reverse. Our findings corroborate
the notion that standard panel regressions, even when adjusted with fixed effects, tend to
bias the magnitude of effects owing to simultaneity concerns. This reinforcement of the dy-
namics between investment, governance, and performance adds nuance to the discourse on
corporate governance effectiveness.
Theory and Contribution: Our paper broadly contributes to the literature on signal-
ing and to the literature on the association between investment and corporate governance.
Although the theoretical foundation of signaling was established by Spence (1973), it was
introduced to finance by Ross (1977). Traditional work on signaling in finance is dominated
6
by dividends, debt ratios, capital expenditure, institutional ownership, ownership concen-
tration, and equity issuances as signals that firms use to mitigate information asymmetry.
Firms differentiate themselves from others in the market by bearing the cost of these signals,
which is shown as separation equilibria in the literature.5 Nevertheless, there is hardly any
evidence in the literature about changes in corporate governance structure, ESG disclosure,
and sustainability reporting as corporate signals.
In this paper, we argue that the adoption of sustainable governance signals to sustain-
able investors the firm’s commitment. Investing in observable signals, such as hiring a chief
sustainability officer (CSO) or forming a CSR/ESG committee, assures investors about the
firm’s sustainability prospects. Firms adopt these governance changes because sustainable
investment (such as green bonds) requires reporting compliance, which includes the devel-
opment of impact reports, use-of-proceeds accounts, and third-party certifications required
under the Green Bond Principles. These governance changes help achieve compliance lev-
els and attain targeted environmental performance. Therefore, incurring the cost of these
governance changes serves as an observable signal to investors that firms are serious about
implementing sustainable projects.
Regarding investment and governance relation, prior literature either focused on how cor-
porate governance mitigates information asymmetry and increases investment (see La Porta
et al. [2000], Gugler et al. [2004]) or on understanding the role of debt holders or institu-
tional investors in corporate governance (see McCahery et al. [2016], Lewellen and Lewellen
[2022]). In the most of these papers, rather than determining these relationships jointly,
they were treated as orthogonal to each other. As corporate governance and firm value are
endogenous, so is corporate governance and investment, since firm value is an important
determinant of the latter. Our paper jointly estimates these relationships and finds that the
impact of investment on governance is stronger than the role of governance in attracting
investment.
Our work also contributes to the emerging literature on sustainable governance. Iliev
and Roth [2023] posit that boards with sustainability expertise not only enhance a firm’s
overall sustainability performance but also increase the likelihood of forming a sustainability
committee. Similarly, Dyck et al. [2023] argues that board renewal mechanisms are essential
for aligning investor preferences with actual environmental sustainability practices within
firms. Their research, which examines the adoption of majority voting for directors and the

aligns with its long-term sustainability transition.
Finally, and most importantly, our work extends the literature on identification through
heteroskedasticity. In the past, this methodology has been used mainly in the macroeco-
nomics literature to understand the impact of monetary policy on asset prices (see Rigobon
and Sack [2003]). We apply this methodology in corporate finance to provide the causal

The influence of sustainable investment on corporate governance could be tempered by
the jurisdiction’s legal environment, particularly regarding shareholder protection rights. In
countries governed by common law, where investor protections are typically robust, the

6.B. Does Sustainable Governance Improve Sustainable Performance?
In the first section, we demonstrate that sustainable debt encourages firms to adopt sus-
tainable governance practices. Since investment and governance decisions are endogenous,
we use Rigobon (2003) methodology to provide causal evidence that the adoption of sustain-
able governance is driven by sustainable investment. It is still essential to examine whether a
firm’s adoption of sustainable governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and
mitigates negative externalities.
We acknowledge that we are not the first to have investigated this question. Dyck et al.
[2023] analyze a global sample of 3,293 firms, demonstrating that quasi-exogenous shocks in
corporate governance—such as the adoption of majority voting for directors and the intro-
duction of a female director—lead to improved future environmental performance. Similarly,
Heath et al. [2023] show that although SRI funds choose portfolio firms based on higher ‘E’
and ‘S’ performances, these funds are inefficient in improving these performances further.
Thus, the real impact of SRI funds is inconsistent with their claimed impact. A recent
theory paper by Starmans et al. [2026] predicts that sustainable investing can weaken the
governance role of financial markets by reducing the sensitivity of stock prices to information
about firm fundamentals, particularly when firm externalities are significant. The authors
hypothesize that pro-social investors would exit firms with weak environmental and social
(E & S) performance even if the firms have exceptional financial performance. It would lead
to a decline in informed trading and would reduce price informativeness and firm’s financial
performance. To compensate, the shareholders must incentivize the manager to improve the
firm’s performance. As incentives are costly, shareholders may choose to reduce these pro-
visions optimally. This would lead to lower managerial effort and would diminish financial
performance.
In contrast to these papers, we investigate whether a firm’s adoption of sustainable gover-
nance, prompted by sustainable investing, drives sustainable performance. We contend that
sustainable governance serves as a complementary monitoring tool alongside shareholder
oversight of a firm’s sustainability efforts. Furthermore, we assert that for firms engaged
in sustainable investing, implementing sustainable governance is unlikely to be merely a
22
marketing strategy, due to the associated costs and the existing monitoring conducted by
pro-social shareholders. With this perspective in mind, we assess the impact of sustainable
governance on the firm’s future sustainable performance. We measure performance using
environmental and ESG scores from the Refinitiv ESG Rating database. The results are
available in Table VI.
Panel A indicates that the regression coefficient of sustainable governance on ESG scores
increases from 0.125 for one-year-ahead scores to 0.151 for five-year-ahead scores. Similarly,
Panel B, which presents results using E-scores, shows an improvement in the coefficient
from 0.149 to 0.192. These findings suggest that sustainable governance positively impacts
sustainable performance, and this effect strengthens over time. Our results indicate that
sustainable investing can enhance a firm’s environmental performance by improving its sus-
tainable governance. These findings align with the work of Dyck et al. [2023] but differ from
the conclusions drawn by Starmans et al. [2026] and Heath et al. [2023]. This discrepancy
may arise because Starmans et al. [2026] and Heath et al. [2023] focus on market governance,
whereas our emphasis is on enhancing in-house sustainable governance.
To show the causal inference of these results, we again use Rigobon (2003). Similar to
the investment on governance model, the simultaneous equations for this model are,
Sus Govt = λ Sus P erft + υt
Sus P erft = ρ Sus Govt + ςt
Here, Sus Govt and Sus P erft are adjusted to country fixed effects and industry fixed
effects before using them for identification through heteroskedasticity.
The problem of identification is that the covariance matrix provides only three moments
- variance of Sus Govt, Sus P erft, and the covariance between Sus Govt and Sus P erft,
whereas there are four unknowns - λ, ρ, σ2 υ and σ2 ς . Therefore, identification through het-
eroskedasticity helps to resolve this issue by dividing the data into regimes where variance
of Sus Govt and Sus P erft are different.
For GMM, Sus P erft is measured as E-Score and ESG-Score at year t and t+1. The
ρE Scoret and ρE Scoret+1 are 0.176 and 0.183. Both the estimates are significant at 1%. Simi-
larly, the ρESG Scoret and ρESG Scoret+1 are 0.161 and 0.159, these estimates are also significant
at 1%. These estimates suggest that sustainable governance improves the environmental per-
23
formance of the firm by 16-18% and these findings are in line with OLS results. Figure VI
(a) - (d) shows the distribution of these γ estimates.
In contrast, we find that GMM estimates for λE Scoret and λE Scoret+1 are insignificant
which implies that firms with better environmental performance have less chance of sustain-
able governance adoption. These results are intuitive as the firms with better environmental
performance would not adopt sustainable governance if the benefits of it are marginal com-
pared to the cost of adoption.
Aswani and Rajgopal [2025] discusses that the environmental performance of green bond
issuers does not capture the performance of financial firms because these firms do not have
environmental externalities of their own but monitor those of sustainable loan borrowers.
Therefore, to conclusively assess environmental performance under sustainable governance,
it is crucial to evaluate borrowers’ performance in light of lenders’ adoption of sustainable
governance. This is also significant because it underscores the lender’s due diligence in
monitoring the borrower’s environmental performance.
To check it empirically, we collect the sustainable loans data from Dealscan. There
are 41,052 sustainable loans issued from 2013-2022. We match this loan data with our main
sample using fuzzy matching based on the lender parent name. For the 1,441 financial firms in
our main sample, we find the match for 178 firms which has issued 54% loans. By gathering
information on total carbon emissions and total carbon intensity for these borrowers, we
investigate the relationship between the lender’s adoption of sustainable governance and the
borrowers’ environmental performance. The empirical specification includes indicators for
the lender’s sustainable governance, deal characteristics, and fixed effects for the borrower’s
country, industry, and borrowing year. Results for this test are in Table VII. We find
no significant impact of the lender’s adoption of sustainable governance on the borrower’s
environmental performance. These results are the same for carbon emissions at the level and
in intensity.
Overall, these results imply that the adoption of sustainable governance affects sustain-
able performance only for non-financial firms; for financial firms, to improve sustainable
performance, there is an additional requirement for monitoring beyond the adoption of sus-
tainable governance.
7. CONCLUSION
This paper examines the dynamics through which sustainable investment motivates firms
to adopt governance structures oriented toward sustainability. Using a global sample of
24
10,970 firms merged with 3,944 sustainable debt issuances, we find that a 1% increase in
sustainable debt issuances raises the likelihood of adopting sustainable governance practices
by 3.7%.
As prior literature has demonstrated that superior corporate governance attracts invest-
ment, we retest this theory and find that improving sustainable governance practices—either
by hiring a chief sustainability officer or establishing an ESG/CSR committee—increases the
amount of sustainable debt issuance by 1%. However, these estimates are biased due to the
simultaneity issue.
To address the simultaneity issue, we employ a Generalized Method of Moments (GMM)
model utilizing a probabilistic instrument based on heteroskedasticity. Our findings reveal
that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (as a proportion of total debt) enhances sustainable
governance by 9.2%. These results remain robust whether we measure sustainable debt
by the number of issuances or the amount issued (scaled by total debt), or when using
alternative ESG databases. These findings suggest that OLS regression, even with fixed
effects, underestimates the coefficients. This core relationship underscores the catalytic role
of financial investment in driving corporate governance reforms.
Our analysis builds upon and diverges from existing literature, such as the study by
Wintoki et al. [2012], which explores the dynamic relationship between board structure
and firm performance but finds no causal linkage. In contrast, our results indicate that
sustainable investment actively promotes better governance, countering the notion of a non-
causal relationship and highlighting the importance of examining these variables within the
context of sustainability.
To enhance the robustness of our findings, we conduct sub-sample analyses based on legal
framework (comparing common law and civil law countries) and sector (contrasting financial
with pollution-intensive industries). While these analyses serve to deepen our understanding,
they reveal that the fundamental relationship between investment and governance remains
significant across different legal and sectoral contexts, albeit with varying magnitudes.
In the second part of the paper, we evaluate whether a firm’s adoption of sustainable
governance effectively streamlines sustainable investment and, more importantly, mitigates
negative externalities, or whether it merely serves as an advertising gimmick supporting
greenwashing claims. We argue that sustainable governance serves as a complementary
monitoring tool alongside shareholder oversight of a firm’s sustainability efforts. Further-
more, we contend that for firms engaged in sustainable investing, implementing sustainable
governance is unlikely to be merely a marketing strategy, given the associated costs and the
25
existing monitoring conducted by pro-social shareholders. With this perspective in mind,
we assess the impact of sustainable governance on the firm’s future sustainable performance.
Our results indicate that sustainable investing can enhance a firm’s environmental perfor-
mance through improvements in sustainable governance.
The findings of this paper reaffirm the significant impact of sustainable debt on gov-
ernance improvements across diverse global settings. However, we acknowledge that the
transformative power of such investments can be influenced by the legal environment and
the operational sector of the firm. Notably, while the core relationship is universal, the ex-
tent of governance enhancement is more pronounced in civil law countries, potentially due
to weaker pre-existing shareholder protections compared to their common law counterparts.
Furthermore, the impact of sustainable debt on governance is more discernible within the
financial sector, likely reflecting the sector’s pivotal role in the transition toward sustainabil-
ity.
Extending our analysis to understand the role of sustainable governance, we find that
sustainable investing can enhance a firm’s environmental performance by improving its sus-
tainable governance. The causal GMM estimates suggest that sustainable governance im-
proves the environmental performance of a firm by 16% to 18%. These results hold only for
non-financial firms; for financial firms, to improve sustainable performance, there is an ad-
ditional requirement for due-diligence beyond adopting sustainable governance. We believe
that these findings contribute to the ongoing debate on relation between sustainable invest-
ment and corporate governance, providing valuable insights for academicians, policymakers,
investors, and corporations striving toward a sustainable future.
